summary: At 36 square miles with fewer than 7,000 residents, Joshua Tree spreads across the high desert at roughly 2,700 feet of elevation with a population density so low — 188 people per square mile — that your nearest neighbor's porch light may be the only thing between you and a horizon of granite monzogranite formations. The city sits at the northwestern gateway to Joshua Tree National Park, which means world-class rock climbing, scrambling, and open-sky stargazing are essentially at the back door, but daily errands are another story: groceries, healthcare, and most services require driving, often down to Yucca Valley or farther into the Morongo Basin. With a median home price around $280,600 against a median household income of roughly $64,000, the price-to-income ratio lands near 4.4× — more accessible than coastal California but tight given that the local economy leans heavily on tourism, small-scale hospitality, and public-sector employment, and the poverty rate sits at 22.6%. Summers push daytime highs well above 100°F while winters drop into genuine cold-desert territory, yet the area averages nearly 11 hours of sunshine daily year-round. Joshua Tree is a place where the extraordinary landscape and the thin economic infrastructure exist in constant, unresolved tension.
